““Little heaven of blessed femininity.” This is a curious expression on a number of counts:

Firs…” —@Genius

children: “Little heaven of blessed femininity.” This is a curious expression on a number of counts:
First, if (as it first appears) it is Molly angrily scolding the camel the expression makes no sense, which, in this episode, it doesn’t necessarily need to.
Second, the expression is part of a phrase Stephen reads in the
Wandering Rocks

episode, where he has picked up a book off a barrow in front of Clohissey’s bookshop on Bedford Row. The book purports to contain “Secrets of secrets,” including “How to win a woman’s love.” The full quote is “Se el yilo nebrakada femininum! Amor me solo! Sanktus! Amen,” or “[My] little heaven of blessed femininity, love only me. Holy! Amen.” So this is Bloom’s hallucination, wherein Molly says something neither she nor Bloom knows anything about.

Third, in spite of the fact that it was Molly who had betrayed Bloom earlier in the day, she is demanding, condescending, and angry. It is Bloom whose self-esteem is at low tide (for now). The ludicrous camel “fumbles to kneel” just as Bloom “stoops his back for leapfrog.” The camel is Bloom.

8736942.twitter_share_message: “The opera Maritana by William Vincent Wallace contains a song “There is a Flower That Bloometh.”…” —@Genius

children: The opera
Maritana
by William Vincent Wallace contains a song “There is a Flower That Bloometh.” The title could not be more pertinent, either for the novel
Ulysses
or for the goings on at this point in
Circe

. The card Bloom has been carrying in his hat since morning, the card bearing the name “Henry Flower” he used as ID to get his letter from Martha Clifford that morning from the post office. This is the “Flower” that “Bloometh.” Now, as defendant in his “trial,” he appears, “holding a fullblown waterlily,” symbol of purity of heart. In the opera, Don Caesar has been tricked into marrying Maritana, and is unhappy, not knowing who she was, veiled as she had been for the ceremony. Maritana is now gone from his life, and he sings, “There is a flower that bloometh / When autumn leaves are shed. /… Oh, pluck it ere it wither, / ‘Tis the memory of the past// It wafted perfume o'er us, / Of sweet, though sad regret / For the true friends gone before us, / Whom none would e’re forget. / Let no heart brave its power, / By guilty thoughts o'ercast, / For then, a poison flow'r / Is – the memory of the past.”
If Bloom ever had true friends, there are none there to defend him. He was washed over in loneliness and the poison flower of guilty thoughts of his bad behavior, the memories of the past.

There is linkage between the Don Caesar/ Maritana couple and the Blooms. Leopold has not known who Molly is (nor, certainly, she him) and he has believed she is now is gone, at least, emotionally, from him forever. “All is lost,” the title to another aria from the opera
Martha
with deep significance to
Ulysses
